    USA v. Thomas Autry (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02490 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02490-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 10, 2026, the Third Circuit affirmed a revocation sentence imposed on Thomas Autry after the district court found a drug offense violation of his supervised release, a Grade A violation. The court held that the 37-month sentence, at the top of the 30-to-37-month Guidelines range, was consistent with 18 U.S.C. § 3583 and Esteras v. United States because the district court did not rely on the retributive factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)(2)(A) and sanctioned the defendant's breach of trust. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:17:18 Eastern time ET
    Timothy Smith v. Social Security Administration, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-02245 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-02245-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 10, 2026, the Third Circuit issued a non-precedential per curiam opinion affirming the Western District of Pennsylvania's dismissal of pro se appellant Timothy Smith's claims against the Social Security Administration, Huntington National Bank, and Northwest Savings Bank. The district court dismissed the claims against the Social Security Administration for failure to state a claim, the claims against Northwest as untimely under the applicable statute of limitations, and the remaining state claims against Huntington for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The Third Circuit found that the appellant's brief did not clearly challenge those grounds, deemed the arguments forfeited, and affirmed after independent review of the record. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:17:18 Eastern time ET
    Zoila Saavedra-Villanueva v. Todd Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca8-24-02918 / USCOURTS-ca8-24-02918-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 10, 2026, the Eighth Circuit Clerk of Court sent counsel a letter stating that the court issued an opinion and entered judgment in appeal No. 24-2918, Zoila Saavedra-Villanueva v.   • Observed at 17:23:12 Eastern time ET
    PPL Electric Utilities, et al v. IBEW Local 1600 (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02623 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02623-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential opinion on November 10, 2026, in PPL Electric Utilities and PPL Services Corporation v. IBEW Local 1600, vacating the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's order that had vacated a labor arbitration award and remanding with instructions to enter an order enforcing the award. The arbitrator had found that PPL violated the collective bargaining agreement by not reimbursing a lineman's $50.00 doctor's note cost, based on the incorporated Pennsylvania Medical Pay Law. The court holds that the arbitrator's interpretation can be rationally derived from the agreement and therefore must be left undisturbed. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:23:12 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Troy Anderson (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02680 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02680-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential opinion on November 10, 2026, in United States v. Troy Eugene Anderson, an appeal from the Western District of Pennsylvania's denial of Anderson's motion to suppress and motion to withdraw his conditional guilty plea to receiving visual depictions of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct. Anderson argued that the state search warrant for his laptop was overbroad, general, and based on material omissions. The court concluded that the warrant was not a general warrant and that the claimed omissions would not have negated probable cause, and it states that it will affirm. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:23:12 Eastern time ET
    Clarence Graham v. USA (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-03425 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-03425-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential per curiam opinion on November 10, 2026, summarily affirming the Middle District of Pennsylvania's dismissal, without prejudice, of pro se appellant Clarence Jamar Graham's 28 U.S.C. § 2241 habeas petition. The court held that Graham's filings challenged the validity of his conviction and sentence, so relief had to be sought by a § 2255 motion in the sentencing district, the Eastern District of North Carolina, and not under § 2241. The opinion also states that Graham's request to transfer the petition back was moot. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:23:12 Eastern time ET
    Jeffrey Russell, et al v. Sharon Taffet, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01060 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01060-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit issued a nonprecedential per curiam opinion on November 10, 2026, in Jeffrey Russell, et al. v. Sharon Taffet, et al., affirming the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's denial of Tracy Williams's motion for reconsideration and her Rule 60(b)(4) motion to void a December 2020 default judgment of over $7 million. The court held that the Rule 60(b)(4) motion, filed in 2025, was not made within a reasonable time because Williams had notice of the litigation in 2016, four years before the default judgment was entered. The court did not reach whether Williams was properly served. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit Court of Appeals issued a non-precedential per curiam order denying David Lettieri's petition for a writ of mandamus, which sought to compel the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey to sever and grant two petitions for relief under 28 U.S.C. § 1651. The court found the petition moot as to severance because the district court had already dismissed the underlying request as frivolous and with prejudice on August 12, 2026, and stated that mandamus is not a substitute for appeal. The order notes that Lettieri may file an appeal of that dismissal by October 13, 2026. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-01316 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-01316-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 10, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit issued an order and judgment in Gasser v. Coffey, affirming a district court ruling that denied Sheryl Coffey's motion to dismiss tort claims under the Colorado Governmental Immunity Act. The panel addressed whether willful and wanton conduct under that Act requires a conscious disregard of a risk of physical danger, and whether the plaintiff, Matthew Gasser, adequately pleaded that Coffey consciously disregarded the danger posed by her allegedly false statements. The order states that it is not binding precedent except under the doctrines of law of the case, res judicata, and collateral estoppel. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 17:23:11 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Mashaq White (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-22-02197 / USCOURTS-ca3-22-02197-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 6, 2026, the Third Circuit issued an opinion in United States v. Mashaq White vacating White's sentence and remanding for resentencing. White had pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm by a convicted felon under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), and the court held that his prior Pennsylvania third-degree felony robbery conviction under 18 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 3701(a)(1)(v) does not qualify as a 'crime of violence' under the enumerated-offenses clause of U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(a). The court reasoned that the Pennsylvania offense reaches conduct broader than generic robbery, so it could not serve as a predicate for the § 2K2.1(a)(1) enhancement. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Michael Abramowitz, et al v. Kari Lake, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-25-05314 / USCOURTS-caDC-25-05314-0

    FAPD-AI: The D.C. Circuit affirmed a permanent injunction barring the U.S. Agency for Global Media from removing Michael Abramowitz as head of Voice of America without the approval of a majority of the International Broadcasting Advisory Board, as required by 22 U.S.C. § 6205(e)(1). The court held that the district court had federal-question jurisdiction over the suit, that the statutory requirements are consistent with Article II, and that the district court had equitable power to enjoin the removal. The appeal arose from defendants' August 2025 removal of Abramowitz after he declined a reassignment to a role in Greenville, North Carolina. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:30 Eastern time ET
    Trevor Young, Jr. v. Rodgina Jones, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-01074 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-01074-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential order, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the entry of judgment on a jury verdict for Lieutenant Rodgina Jones and Officer Jacob Martin in a pretrial detainee's Fourteenth Amendment excessive-force suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, arising from a January 2022 taser incident at the Milwaukee County Jail. The court found no abuse of discretion in excluding the jail's use-of-force policies under Federal Rule of Evidence 403 and in admitting Lieutenant Hannah Alexander's testimony about malfunctioning tasers and inaccurate taser logs under Rule 701. The court held that the plaintiff had waived his challenge to the impeachment use of his medical records under Rule 608(b) and his weight-of-the-evidence challenge by not filing a post-trial motion. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:30 Eastern time ET
    Robert Panton v. Todd W. Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02528 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02528-0

    FAPD-AI: The Seventh Circuit granted Robert Panton's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision denying his motion to reopen his removal proceedings, and remanded the case to the Board. Panton, a lawful permanent resident admitted in 1970 who was convicted of a drug conspiracy and removed to Jamaica, had sought reopening to submit a December 2023 New York Police Department certification in support of a waiver of inadmissibility. The court identified errors in the Board's decision, including a statement that Panton had not claimed an exception to the 90-day filing deadline and conflation of a U visa with a waiver of inadmissibility, and noted the government's counsel conceded partial error; on remand the Board must address Panton's arguments but need not reconsider sua sponte reopening. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:29 Eastern time ET
    In re: E. Palestine Train Derailment (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-03499 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-03499-0

    FAPD-AI: In a published opinion, the Sixth Circuit addressed an appeal by 196 East Palestine, Ohio residents who had signed personal-injury releases in exchange for additional payments under a $600 million class settlement with Norfolk Southern, and who moved under Rule 60 for relief from the settlement approval. The movants alleged that class counsel committed fraud on the court, including by describing expert Dr. Carson as 'completely independent,' and that Norfolk Southern had defrauded them. The court concluded that the Rule 60(d)(3) fraud-on-the-court argument and the Rule 60(b)(3) argument did not meet the required showing, and it found that class counsel's statement to the court that it had not retained Carson was not fraudulent. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:29 Eastern time ET
    Gannett Company, Inc., et al v. Jeff Long, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-05182 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-05182-0

    FAPD-AI: The Sixth Circuit vacated the Middle District of Tennessee's February 2026 order denying a preliminary injunction sought by news organizations against enforcement of Tennessee's police buffer-zone statute, Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-16-612, which prohibits approaching within 25 feet of officers in specified circumstances after an order to retreat. The court held that the plaintiffs had standing at this stage and that the district court's irreparable-harm analysis was premature because it did not address likelihood of success on the merits, which the court described as the most important factor in First Amendment cases. The case was remanded for the district court to develop a factual record on the merits and the remaining injunction factors. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:28 Eastern time ET
    Stefanie Boone v. Lowell Area Schools, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-01948 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-01948-0

    FAPD-AI: In a published opinion dated November 10, 2026, the Sixth Circuit reviewed the Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 action brought by Stefanie Boone against Lowell Area Schools and several of its administrators in their official capacities. The action concerned a January 19, 2024 letter from a high school principal requesting that the plaintiff stop referencing District employees on social media and limiting contact with District staff. The court held that a First Amendment claim against the School District was plausibly pleaded, while the Fourteenth Amendment and Title IX claims were not, and it affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for further proceedings, with one judge concurring in part and dissenting in part in a separate opinion. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:28 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Leticia Gallarzo (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-01119 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-01119-0

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed a 75-month sentence imposed on Leticia Gallarzo, who pleaded guilty to aggravated identity theft and to false statements relating to healthcare matters after obtaining nursing employment using another nurse's license number. The court held that the district court did not clearly err in applying a two-level enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1(b)(16)(A) based on a finding that her conduct created a risk of death or serious bodily injury. The court relied on the record, including her duties administering narcotics, starting IV lines, and pulling PICC lines, and a performance-based demotion. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:26 Eastern time ET
    Tyrelle Henderson, Jr. v. Kent County, MI, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-01845 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-01845-0

    FAPD-AI: In a published opinion dated November 10, 2026, the Sixth Circuit reviewed the denial of in forma pauperis status to Tyrelle Motray Henderson, Jr., a Michigan state prisoner suing Kent County, Michigan, and a county sheriff. The court held that dismissals based on Eleventh Amendment immunity do not generally count as strikes under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(g), that the two challenged prior actions therefore did not qualify as strikes, and that issue preclusion did not bar the challenge. The court vacated the district court's order and remanded the case. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:25 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Romero Blount (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-50836 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-50836-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit granted the Government's motion in part and vacated two standard conditions of supervised release, listed as conditions 15 and 16 in the written judgment, imposed on Jorge Ivan Romero Blount after he pleaded guilty to illegal reentry and was sentenced to 30 months of imprisonment and three years of supervised release. The court agreed with the parties that these conditions did not comply with 18 U.S.C. § 3583(d), affirmed the judgment in all other respects, and remanded for entry of an amended written judgment. The court denied the Government's motion in all other respects, including its request for summary affirmance. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:25 Eastern time ET
    Gore v. State Farm (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-60625 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-60625-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for State Farm Fire and Casualty Company in an action brought by Wendy Gore arising from a March 9, 2023 fire at her home in Cleveland, Mississippi. The court held that Gore forfeited her arguments by failing to cite the record adequately, that her breach of contract claims for structural and personal property losses failed, and that her bad faith, negligent misrepresentation, and privacy claims also failed under Mississippi law. The district court had dismissed all claims except breach of contract for living expenses, which Gore later voluntarily dismissed by stipulation, producing a final judgment. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam decision dated November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit reviewed an appeal by Clemente Suarez Alamo from a judgment of the Northern District of Texas.     USA v. Moreno-Lopez (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-50354 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-50354-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam decision dated November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit reviewed an appeal by Raul Alfonso Moreno-Lopez of a conviction and sentence for illegal reentry under 8 U.S.C. § 1326(a). The appellant argued for the first time that the § 1326(b) enhancement is unconstitutional, a challenge the parties agreed is foreclosed by Almendarez-Torres v. United States. The court granted the Government's motion for summary affirmance, denied its alternative motion for an extension of time, and affirmed the district court's judgment. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Thomas v. Whalen (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-50371 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-50371-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam order dated November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit considered a motion by Joshua Greg Thomas to proceed in forma pauperis on appeal from the dismissal of a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint. The court found that the appeal raised no nonfrivolous issue, denied the motion, and dismissed the appeal as frivolous. The court counted the district court's dismissal and the appellate dismissal as two strikes under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(g) and warned that a third strike would bar in forma pauperis filings while the appellant is incarcerated, absent imminent danger of serious physical injury. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    In re: Application (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-26-04303 / USCOURTS-ca4-26-04303-0

    FAPD-AI: In a published opinion filed November 10, 2026, the Fourth Circuit, in the matter In re: Application of the United States of America for an Order Pursuant to 18 U.S.C. Section 2703(d), affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. The appeal concerns a Disclosure Order under 18 U.S.C. § 2703(d) directing LinkedIn to produce metadata for accounts of targeted journalists over an eighteen-month period, and a Secrecy Order under 18 U.S.C. § 2705(b) barring disclosure of the Disclosure Order for one year, both of which LinkedIn moved to modify as overbroad. The court declined to quash the orders entirely and remanded to the district court to narrow them to conform with the Stored Communications Act, 18 U.S.C. §§ 2701-2713, and constitutional norms. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:24 Eastern time ET
    Pettieway v. Supervisor Kelly (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-30714 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-30714-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction the appeal of Marlon James Pettieway, whose 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim had been resolved on summary judgment. The court determined that the notice of appeal, filed November 24, 2025, was untimely under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(1)(A) because judgment was entered October 10, 2025, and that Pettieway's October 15, 2025 filing titled 'Objection' to a magistrate judge's report and recommendation did not constitute a timely notice of appeal even when construed liberally. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:24 Eastern time ET
    Nolan v. Buchanan (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-30724 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-30724-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 10, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of Antonio Lashun Nolan's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit as frivolous and for failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), and denied Nolan's motions concerning the caption and coding of his case. The court held that the magistrate judge's use of a questionnaire and instruction not to repeat prior allegations did not violate due process, and that the Heck v. Humphrey favorable-termination rule barred the claims. The court also held that any challenge not raised on appeal was forfeited. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:23 Eastern time ET
    Bass v. US (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01912 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01912-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of Robert C. Bass's amended complaint, which sought funds from a $15,821,000 forfeiture obtained from the Swiss bank Wegelin & Co. The court held that the claims accrued in 2013 and are time-barred under 28 U.S.C. § 2501, concluding that the accrual suspension rule did not apply because the forfeiture was widely reported and Bass could reasonably have known of his claim by 2013. The court did not reach Bass's remaining arguments, and the per curiam disposition was decided November 10, 2026. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:23 Eastern time ET
    Zahler v. US (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01948 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01948-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction of Jordan Zahler's complaint, which sought $690,226,256 from the United States on the theory that a district court clerk failed to enter default. The court held that the Rules Enabling Act and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 55(a) are not money-mandating sources of law sufficient to support Tucker Act jurisdiction. The court further concluded that the claim essentially sought review of a district court decision, and the disposition was decided November 10, 2026. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:23 Eastern time ET
    US v. Anthony Lynch (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-24-04343 / USCOURTS-ca4-24-04343-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 10, 2026, the Fourth Circuit affirmed in part and dismissed in part the appeal of Anthony Lynch, who pleaded guilty under a plea agreement to attempted enticement of a minor under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b) and to a felony offense involving a minor while required to register as a sex offender under 18 U.S.C. § 2260A, and who was sentenced to 300 months' imprisonment. The court held that the appellate waiver in the plea agreement was valid and enforceable and barred review of the sentencing issues, but that the challenge to the denial of the motion to withdraw the guilty plea fell outside the waiver. The court found that the district court's failure to advise Lynch of the right to appointed counsel at every other stage under Fed. R. Crim. P. 11(b)(1)(D) did not affect his substantial rights, and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in denying the withdrawal motion. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:22 Eastern time ET
    McCaster v. US (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01509 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01509-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit dismissed in part for lack of jurisdiction the appeal of Matthew-Allen McCaster, who sought to proceed on behalf of The Mathias El Tribe under the Indian Tucker Act, because the notice of appeal was untimely as to the August 11, 2025 judgment and the October 23, 2025 order. The court affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' February 19, 2026 order denying his motion to reopen and correct the record, holding that a non-lawyer may not represent an entity such as a tribe and that only a tribe, band, or identifiable group may sue under 28 U.S.C. § 1505. The court also denied the appellant's request to change the caption to name the Tribe as plaintiff-appellant. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:22 Eastern time ET
    Holland v. Collins (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01574 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01574-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction the appeal of Lee Holland, Jr., who challenged a decision of the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims that dismissed his appeal of a Board of Veterans' Appeals decision. The Veterans Court had found the notice of appeal untimely as to the dismissed claims and found no final decision as to the remanded claims. The Federal Circuit stated that it may not review the Veterans Court's application of equitable tolling to the facts, and that labeling the remanded-claims arguments as due process claims does not confer jurisdiction. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:22 Eastern time ET
    Ciers v. MSPB (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01767 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01767-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction of RaShawn Ciers's petition concerning an alleged failure to restore following his 2010 removal from the U.S. Postal Service. The court found that the removal was for cause substantially unrelated to a compensable injury and that his post-removal call center appointment was never formalized, so he was not entitled to restoration rights under 5 C.F.R. §§ 353.301(d) and 353.304. The per curiam disposition, which is nonprecedential, was decided November 10, 2026. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:21 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Alexander Leszczynski (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13074 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13074-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit opinion addresses Alexander Leszczynski's appeal of a 168-month below-guidelines sentence for wire and bank fraud, in which he argues that the district court clearly erred in denying a two-level acceptance-of-responsibility reduction and that the sentence is substantively unreasonable. The opinion recounts the case history, including his attempts to withdraw a guilty plea, the presentence report's obstruction enhancement and resulting 210 to 262 month guidelines range, and the district court's downward variance and consecutive sentence to a separate murder-for-hire sentence. The text available ends during the court's discussion of the acceptance-of-responsibility issue, so the disposition is not stated in the provided excerpt. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:21 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Brandon Parsons (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13141 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13141-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed Brandon Parsons's 600-month total sentence, a downward variance from a guidelines life term, for attempted coercion and enticement of a minor, attempted production of child pornography, distribution and possession of child pornography, and attempted transfer of obscene material to a minor. Parsons argued that the sentence was substantively unreasonable because the district court improperly weighed the 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors and gave insufficient weight to his military service and childhood trauma. The court held that the district court did not commit a clear error of judgment in weighing the factors and noted that a sentence well below the statutory maximum indicates reasonableness. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:21 Eastern time ET
    The National Association of Realtors, et al v. James Mullis, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-11566 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-11566-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction an appeal by non-named class members from a partial final judgment approving settlements for four defendants in a class action brought by home sellers against national real estate brokerages. The court held that the district court's Rule 54(b) certification was improper because the district court gave no reasoning for its no-just-reason-for-delay determination and the remaining claims arose from the same operative facts. The opinion notes that after the district court dismisses the remaining defendants with prejudice, a final, appealable judgment will exist. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01233 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01233-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal under RCFC 12(b)(6) of Diansky Rouzard's suit seeking refunds of federal income tax for the 2019 and 2022 tax years. The court held that Rouzard did not plausibly allege that he duly filed administrative refund claims under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), because the documents he submitted did not establish the claimed overpayments. The per curiam disposition, which is nonprecedential, was decided November 10, 2026. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:20 Eastern time ET
    Michael Fitzgerald, et al v. Ronda McNae (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-11685 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-11685-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed a district court judgment in favor of Michael Fitzgerald against Ronda McNae for breach of a confidential settlement agreement, under which Fitzgerald paid $97,000 in exchange for non-disparagement and confidentiality promises. The district court granted summary judgment on liability and, after a bench trial on damages, awarded $2,746,703.27 in economic and noneconomic damages. The opinion addresses McNae's arguments concerning Florida law and public policy, the First Amendment, the damages award, and a remedy based on trial counsel's alleged ineffectiveness, and finds no merit in them. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:02:20 Eastern time ET
    Everett Smith v. Warden, Dooly SP (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12556 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12556-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Everett Smith's pro se 28 U.S.C. § 2254 habeas petition, which challenged his state life sentence for aggravated sexual battery and child molestation. Smith argued that trial counsel was ineffective under Strickland v. Washington for interrupting his testimony, not calling his mother and sister as witnesses, and failing to timely subpoena a Georgia DFCS employee. The court applied AEDPA deference, concluded that the challenged choices were strategic or not prejudicial, and found that Smith had not shown the state court's ruling was contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established federal law. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit, in a non-argument per curiam opinion, affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment to the Secretary of the Air Force on pro se appellant Cecile Jackson's race and gender discrimination and retaliation claims under Title VII. Res. 1650, a closed rule providing for consideration of H.R. 1013, the Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act of 2025, with one hour of general debate and one motion to recommit. The resolution waives points of order against the bill and provides that the Committee on Financial Services substitute be considered as adopted. During debate, Representative Griffith described the bill as allowing 403(b) plans the option to invest in collective investment trusts, while Representative McGovern criticized the scheduling of the bill.     Raising a Question of the Privileges of the House (opens in a new tab)
    Congressional Record · govinfo API · CREC-2026-11-10 / CREC-2026-11-10-pt1-PgH6126-3

    FAPD-AI: Representative Massie raised a question of the privileges of the House and offered H. Res. 1655, which would impeach Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, and exhibit articles of impeachment to the Senate. Article I cites Section 2(c) and Article II cites Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, asserting that military hostilities against Iran beginning February 28, 2026, lacked a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency, and that continued operations after House Concurrent Resolution 86 was agreed to by both chambers on June 3 and June 23, 2026, violated Section 5(c).
